findings.element: state=print — states.print in render-b.js:1249 (min-height:1123px), .b-print and the @container (min-width: 600px) rule at b.css:1111
findings.problem: Driven at the sheet's real size, the one artifact that cannot be reflowed after it exists is not the size it says it is. states.print declares A4 as 1123px and then overflows it at every width. At a 794px viewport — A4 at 96dpi — .tl-paperEdge measures 714 x 1828, and at 768 it is 688 x 1828: 1.63 sheets. The two-column composition every frame in this lab shows only exists at a 1280 or 1440 viewport, where the paper finally gets its full 794px and .b-print's content box reaches 664; at a real 794px sheet that content box is 584, sixteen pixels under the 600 threshold, so the container query never fires and the keepsake silently stacks into one long column. Even in the composition the panel has been shown, it is 794 x 1442 against A4's 1123 — 319px, 28 percent, over. There is no @page rule and no @media print anywhere in b.css or shell.css, so the 56/64/44 margins the composition declares are not the margins the sheet gets either. What actually comes out of a home printer is two sheets, the second holding the share link and the footer alone. On the morning itself somebody hands that to a guest.
findings.fix: In render-b.js states.print change min-height:1123px to height:1123px so the overflow is visible in the lab instead of silent. Drop the container threshold at b.css:1111 from 600px to 560px so the two-column composition holds at the real sheet width. Then take the 319px out of the measure, not the margins: set SCALE.print in render-b.js:33 from 10 to 5 — the printed span runs day 16 to day 79, so 63 days at 10px is 630px and at 5px is 315px, which lands the paper at 1127px, inside A4 with the proportion between every gap unchanged. Finally add @page { size: A4; margin: 0 } and an @media print block that hides the lab caption so the sheet carries the composition's own margins.

findings.problem: The link card was fixed this round to announce when its figure was true: the unfurl reads "79 · days away when this was sent" (render-b.js:1135). Paper, which can be corrected even less than a cached preview, was not. The keepsake's largest object by a factor of five is "79", captioned only "days", and the sheet then stamps itself "Today is 16 July" — a sentence that is false from midnight and cannot be edited. Underneath it the footer carries a second date in a second grammar, "UPDATED 15 JULY 2026", one day apart from the first, so the reader holding the page has two dates and no way to tell which one dates the paper. Three time facts, two grammars, one object that can never be right about any of them again. Meanwhile the one fact the sheet will still be right about in October — Saturday 3 October 2026 — is set at 30px, a fifth the height of the number that expires overnight.
findings.fix: In render-b.js states.print, pass the print measure a dated caption in the unfurl's own grammar: set .b-away on print to "days away on 16 July 2026" built from F.fmt.longYear(F.today) rather than the bare "days". Delete .b-todayLabel and its .b-todayRule from the print state only — the caption now dates the sheet, and the sheet's single indigo mark moves to the horizon date. Change the footer's middle cell from "UPDATED " + updated to "PRINTED 16 JULY 2026" from the same accessor, so the sheet carries exactly one date about itself. Keep the order and the sizes; the lock owns those.

findings.problem: The keepsake's only route back to the living plan is a 101-character line ending in a 43-character random token, set at 13px Geist Mono, wrapping across three lines at the real sheet width. Round 4 fixed its case so it could in principle be typed; nobody asked whether it would be. It will not be. A guest at a wedding holding a printed page does not transcribe forty-three mixed-case characters into a phone, and the one they mistype lands nowhere. So the sheet's closing sentence is a promise the object cannot keep, printed in the product's own machine voice at the exact moment the keepsake should feel like a card rather than a receipt.
findings.fix: Replace the raw URL line with a QR block: a 96px square of the same ink on the same paper, sitting in the left column under the horizon where the sheet already carries 700px of empty rail, captioned in 11px mono with "Scan for the live plan" and, below it in the same colour, the bare host "timeline.signalstudio.ie". Keep the full URL in the element's accessible name and in the anchor's href so a copy of the file still carries it. No new hue, no new weight, and it uses space the sheet is already wasting.

findings.element: shell.css token block vs the 69 raw font-size declarations in b.css
findings.problem: Asked whether a second product can be built from this without copying this one: almost. shell.css already names four of the five ladders a language needs — the ink ladder (--ink-04 through --ink-90 with its --fore/--back inversion), leading by role (--lead-display / head / title / body / date / label), tracking by role, the space ladder (--gap-hair through --gap-page) and the motion ladder with one easing. Home, Notes and Tasks could wear all of that tomorrow. The fifth ladder, the one the language is most defined by, is not named anywhere: type size lives as 69 raw pixel literals across b.css in thirteen distinct steps (11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 20, 24, 30, 38, 48, 64, 96, 148), none of which has a name, a role or a home in shell.css. So the first thing a second product needs is the one thing it would have to reverse-engineer by grepping this product's stylesheet and guessing which of thirteen numbers is a title. Nor does the language have a name: "B · The Approach" names a direction in a lab, not a system a founder can tell three teams to adopt.
findings.fix: Move the ramp into shell.css as role tokens beside the leading tokens it already pairs with — --size-display 148/96, --size-figure 64/48, --size-head 38/30, --size-title 24/20, --size-body 17/15, --size-meta 13/12, --size-label 11 — and replace the 69 literals in b.css with them, so every size arrives with the leading and tracking that belong to it. Then write one page, docs/design/labs/timeline-redesign-2026-08/LANGUAGE.md, that names the system and states the five ladders plus the four rules that are not tokens: three colours, two weights, condition by ink density, one accent per screen and it is always on what is next. That page plus shell.css is what Home, Notes and Tasks inherit; b.css stays Timeline's.

findings.element: .b-behindLabel — render-b.js:337, dayOf ternary; aria-label at render-b.js:390
findings.problem: Still two names for one object, and the panel's own round-4 refuter endorsed fixing it and it was not done. Driven at 390: ?state=phone and ?state=print head the block "BEHIND YOU"; ?state=day heads the same block, same content, same treatment, "HOW YOU GOT HERE". A guest who opened the link in July and opens it again on the morning meets a section that has been renamed under them. The aria-label at line 390 is a third variant, hard-coded to "How you got here" even on the surfaces that read "Behind you", so the visible and the announced names disagree on every guest surface except the day. One name per thing is this seat's floor, and it is the only naming inconsistency left on the guest side.
findings.fix: Delete the dayOf ternary at render-b.js:337 so .b-behindLabel is "Behind you" everywhere, and set the aria-label at line 390 to "Behind you, most recent first". Then add an assertion to interaction-check.mjs that .b-behindLabel is byte-identical on ?state=day and ?state=phone, exactly as the round-4 refuter specified.

biggestWin: The owner's voice is now the best writing in the company and the guest surfaces have caught most of the way up. "Nothing is planned until 1 August.", "This link has stopped working." with "Nothing has been deleted. Only the link stopped working." under it, "kept by Orla", and "79 days away when this was sent" are declarative, concrete, unhedged and free of both jargon and reassurance — the ended screen in particular now says only what it can know, which is the hardest sentence in the product to get right, and it is right. The palette is spent rather than obeyed: one indigo mark per screen, always on the thing that is next, so three colours read as conviction instead of constraint. What stands between this and 9.5 is not the screens, it is the sheet. The printed keepsake is the only object this product makes that cannot be fixed after it exists, and driven at real A4 it is not A4 — 1442px against 1123 in the composition the panel has been shown, 1828 and single-column at the width it is actually printed, closing on a forty-three character token no guest will ever type, under a number that is false by morning. That is roughly two days: one to make the sheet a sheet, half a day for the QR and the dated caption, half a day to lift the type ramp into shell.css and write the one page that names the language — without which Home, Notes and Tasks will inherit this product by copying its stylesheet rather than by wearing its system.
